def: A tag that also stores a message, the tagger's name and a date. Created with git tag -a. Preferred for releases.
A movable label pointing to a commit, used to work on something in parallel without disturbing main.
A full copy of a repository, with all files and history, downloaded to your computer with git clone. The original becomes the remote 'origin'.
A person given permission to push to a GitHub repository (Settings → Collaborators).
A saved snapshot of the project, with an author, date, message and a link to its parent commit(s).
The unique 40-character ID of a commit (e.g. 6cb774b…). Usually shown shortened to 7 characters.
The text describing what a commit does and why. Good messages start with a verb: 'Add vada pav to menu'.
When two branches changed the same lines, Git can't merge automatically. It marks both versions in the file and asks you to choose.
The tool installed with Git for Windows that signs you in to GitHub through the browser and remembers the login.
The state when HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch, e.g. after git checkout <commit>. Return with git switch main.
A line-by-line comparison showing what changed: lines starting with - were removed, + were added. Shown by git diff and git show.
A VCS where every copy of a repository holds the full history, so you can work offline and any copy can restore the others. Git is distributed.
A VCS where one central server holds the only full history; clients depend on it. Examples: CVS, SVN.
A merge where the receiving branch had no new commits, so Git just moves its label forward. No merge commit is created.
Download new commits from a remote into remote-tracking branches (e.g. origin/main) without changing your branch or files.
Your own copy of someone else's repository, on GitHub, under your account. Used to propose changes with a pull request.
A file listing patterns of files Git should not track, such as passwords, build output or node_modules/.
Free, open-source distributed version control software that runs on your computer. Created by Linus Torvalds in 2005.
The terminal installed with Git for Windows. It understands Linux-style commands such as ls, cd and pwd.
A website that hosts Git repositories and adds teamwork features: issues, pull requests, forks, reviews and more.
Git's pointer to where you are now: usually the current branch (shown in the prompt as (main)).
A numbered GitHub discussion about one task: a bug, a feature request or a question.
The repository on your own computer: the .git folder with the full history.
Bring the commits of one branch into another. Results in a fast-forward or a merge commit.
A commit with two parents, created when two branches that both moved on are joined.
The default name of the remote repository you cloned from or pushed to first (usually your GitHub repository).
git fetch followed by git merge: download the team's new commits and merge them into your current branch.
A GitHub request to review a branch and merge it into another branch, usually main.
Upload your commits to a remote repository such as GitHub.
The project's front page: a Markdown file explaining what the project is and how to use it. GitHub shows it below the file list.
A named copy of the repository on another computer or server, such as GitHub. Managed with git remote.
Git's read-only bookmark of where a remote branch was at your last fetch, pull or push, e.g. origin/main.
A project tracked by Git: the files plus their complete history (stored in the .git folder).
Move the current branch back to an earlier commit. --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstaged, --hard deletes them.
Discard uncommitted edits in a file (git restore file) or unstage it (git restore --staged file).
Create a new commit that undoes an earlier one. Safe for commits already pushed, because history is kept.
The very first commit in a repository; it has no parent.
The list of changes chosen for the next commit. git add puts changes here; also called the index.
A GitHub bookmark for a repository you like; the number of stars shows popularity.
Temporarily park uncommitted changes so the working tree is clean; bring them back with git stash pop.
A permanent name for a commit, usually a release such as v1.0. Unlike a branch, it never moves.
A file Git already knows about (it was added and committed). New files are untracked until you git add them.
A second login step (a code from an app or phone) that protects your GitHub account even if your password leaks.
A file in your folder that Git has never saved. git status lists it under 'Untracked files'.
The remote branch your local branch tracks (set with git push -u). In forks, 'upstream' also names the original repository.
Software that records changes to files over time, so you can see who changed what and bring back earlier versions.
The files you see and edit in your project folder.
